Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

crime noun

also crimes, offence, offense, commit a crime, wrongdoing, offences

classical

Cic. Verr. 2.5.170
Cic. Cat. 2.27
Traupman 194
Traupman 194: commit a crime, scelus committere

scelus, sceleris n.

noun, third declension

a crime, a wicked deed

The strongest general word for a wicked act (Lewis & Short). To commit a crime, scelus committere (Traupman 194) or admittere (Cic. Att. 9.10.3, Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • facinus, facinoris n. — a misdeed, a crime; in comedy also simply a deed

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Verr. 2.5.170; Caes. BG 7.38.8: nefāriō facinore admissō (Lewis & Short); Traupman 194

  • maleficium, maleficiī n. — an offence, a crime

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Caec. 6; Cic. Rosc. Am. 62: maleficium committere (Lewis & Short)

    The law’s word for a criminal act, as in Cicero’s pūniendōrum maleficiōrum causā.

  • dēlictum, dēlictī n. — a fault, a lesser offence

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.145; Traupman 196: dēlicta, offences

  • crīmen, crīminis n. — a crime (mostly in poets and later prose); classically the charge

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Lucr. 3.49 (Lewis & Short); Liv. 40.12.10 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 194

    Above all the accusation (see charge); the sense ‘crime’ is rare in prose before Augustus (Lewis & Short). Traupman: “more often means merely the charge”.

Examples

  • Facinus est vincīre cīvem Rōmānum, scelus verberāre, prope parricīdium necāre

    It is a crime to bind a Roman citizen, a wickedness to flog him, almost parricide to kill himCic. Verr. 2.5.170

  • ex eā cāritāte quae est inter nātōs et parentēs, quae dirimī nisi dētestābilī scelere nōn potest

    the love between children and parents, which nothing but a hateful crime can breakCic. Amic. 27

See also criminal, punishment, steal, law, charge.
